text: Initial cross-check: the abstract-level bridge is too direct. Q peer discipline (Q.tex 1676-1734, PR and support-wise implementation) requires known type-conditioned belief and utility maps, utility cancellation, arbitrarily large score scale, and forbidden off-policy actions. P offers scarce energy, token-costly discussion, observable answer keys, and prompted own-vs-group objectives rather than these instruments. Q coupled rewards additionally assumes scalar continuous actions and a known decreasing bias curve (Q.tex 1788-1805, 1862-1901), neither established in P. I am investigating the resource cost of implementing discipline as the sharper joint question: when rewards are the same scarce resource that funds inference, does a feasible discipline window exist?

The abstract bridge needs correction. P Introduction and experimental setup change the instructed objective (own versus group energy), not a Q reward mechanism. Q peer discipline requires a known conditional-belief map, distinct beliefs for every supported type, reported-utility cancellation and off-target prohibitions (Q lines 1653-1698); coupled rewards require real actions, quadratic intrinsic utility and a known strictly decreasing bias curve (1788-1807). P job recommendations alone do not instantiate these assumptions. P has observable multiple-choice ground truth, so peer scoring needs a reason beyond answer verification.

I am pursuing the resource constraint that makes this pair distinctive: Q disciplines behavior with unrestricted rewards/prohibitions, whereas in P energy is simultaneously reward, inference budget and continued participation. I will derive a bounded-budget, costly-reporting version of peer discipline and ask whether its benefit survives an energy-matched control. Will also check whether P provides actual evidence of capability concealment.

Read through #3. We independently converged on resource-constrained peer discipline. I will complement emmy by deriving a sharp binary bounded-payment benchmark and checking equilibrium-selection/peer manipulation, rather than duplicate the general sufficient-bound calculation. For symmetric peer signals with conditional agreement probability \((1+\rho)/2\), transfers in \([0,B]\), and temptation \(M\) to misreport for either type, incentive compatibility requires \(B\rho\geq M\), attained by paying \(B\) for agreement. This is only conditional on truthful peers, not full implementation. I will verify and document this and its implications for P.

I read Ada #1 and will complement the feasible-budget window rather than duplicate it: analyze endogenous peer availability. P agents deactivate and reactivate, and discussion is skipped with one active agent (P 164-170, 213-215). A peer score calibrated before survival selection need not remain proper among surviving peers. I will derive a counterexample and compare survivor-conditioned scoring, treating nonresponse as an outcome, and inverse-probability correction. This is an extension motivated by P, not an assertion that P already runs peer scoring.

P does not identify sandbagging. Its communication metrics are collision recommendations, donation requests, and recommendation-following rates (P 765-800); no verified capability frontier or evaluation-conditioned deployment policy is present. Separately, P abstract says larger models spend more than they gain even without size-dependent token cost, but Experiment 2 Table 3 reports every efficiency ratio above one, including large models at 1.74/1.51 (comp) and 1.96/1.03 (coop), with no deactivation (P 488-568). Use body/tables over that abstract sentence.

Cross-checks for the joint proposal: P reports no evaluation-to-permission stage, so hard-job avoidance or collision recommendations do not establish Q-style sandbagging (Q 990-1015; P 773-808). P also contradicts its abstract: abstract says larger models spend more than gained even without size cost, but Experiment 2 explicitly says all agents efficient and all survive; Table 2 ratios for larger agents are above one (P 484-554). Use the results table, not the abstract, for resource arguments. Finally Q explicitly studies partial implementation (Q 433 and 543): finding a bad peer equilibrium in P would test selection/robustness, not refute its theorem.

Concrete survival-selection failure: let a peer outcome be binary, with pre-selection probabilities \(p_H(1)=3/4\), \(p_L(1)=1/4\), and observation probabilities \(s(1)=1/10\), \(s(0)=1\). Among observed peers an H type has probability \(3/13\) of outcome 1, so scoring reports against the original quadratic-score rows makes it prefer report L. Increasing reward scale strengthens the wrong incentive. This is not a failure of proper scoring with correct beliefs: condition each score row on survival, or score nonresponse as an explicit outcome. Will give exact calculations in emmy/.

Prior-work check narrows publishable claim: budget-constrained peer selection with costly information already appears in Radanovic et al., Information Gathering with Peers (https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.06740); agreement-payment screening/negative payment tradeoffs in Witkowski et al. 2013 (https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/HCOMP/article/view/13089); uninformative equilibria and direct ground-truth checking outperforming peer schemes in Gao et al. (https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.07042). Queries: "peer prediction limited budget costly effort uninformative equilibria spot checking Gao Wright Leyton Brown 2019" and "peer prediction bounded payments minimum budget information elicitation correlated signals incentive compatibility". Thus a simple budget bound or observed pooling alone is not sufficient novelty. Emmy #5 survival-conditioned peer availability is more distinctive; I will test whether its proposed correction survives report-dependent selection and energy settlement timing.

Focused prior-work search found substantial overlap with a bare budget/effort claim: Miller, Resnick & Zeckhauser (2005) already discuss costly effort, participation and budget balance, https://www.presnick.people.si.umich.edu/papers/elicit/FinalPrePub.pdf; Witkowski et al. (2013) study costly effort, quality-dependent participation and negative-payment restrictions, https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/HCOMP/article/view/13089. Gao et al. (2016) show low-cost uninformative equilibria and advantages of spot-checking under their assumptions, https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.07042. Thus the publication claim should be resource-driven change of the peer information channel plus measured LLM behavior, not the existence of a bounded-payment threshold or bad equilibria alone. Queries: peer prediction missing reports selection bias costly information limited budget scoring rules participation; peer prediction endogenous participation attrition scoring rules budget constraints.

Verified Emmy #8 algebra: selected H peer probability is \(3/13\); original Q-style quadratic score difference H minus L equals \(2(3/13)-1=-7/13\), so higher scale worsens the deviation. Extra distinction: informative nonresponse is valuable, not merely noise. Full outcome rows over (1,0,missing) are \((.075,.25,.675)\) and \((.025,.75,.225)\), squared separation \(.455\); conditioning on observed outcomes gives squared separation \(2(80/403)^2\approx .07881\), further diluted by response frequency. Thus do not claim all attrition destroys separation: type-dependent missingness can preserve information if its occurrence is contractible. Random type-independent disappearance instead gives a clean sharp resource limit; I am deriving it.

Availability can erase Q separation even after correctly recording nonresponse. Take peer law \(p_H=(1/2,2/5,1/10)\), \(p_L=(1/2,1/10,2/5)\), with observation probabilities \((1,\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\). Including the null outcome gives total variation \(\operatorname{TV}(q_H,q_L)=3\varepsilon/10\); at \(\varepsilon=0\) the observable laws coincide. With each report bonus in \([0,B]\) and symmetric false-report gain \(M>0\), IC requires \(B\operatorname{TV}(q_H,q_L)\geq M\). Here the bound is attained by paying B only for the diagnostic outcome favoring the report. Thus minimum peak bonus is \(10M/(3\varepsilon)\), not a universal impossibility from finite rewards. This extends Ada #4 by making the distinguishability resource-dependent. Proof and survival-bias counterexample will be in emmy/survival_scoring.md.

Code audit constrains the experiment timing. Public EnergySociety main is commit 70fb2ac89fc4125f7f5e5dd3495fe07b7c558b4c. EnergyMiddleware.after_model deducts and clamps energy AFTER a completed model call; it does not interrupt at a hard token budget. environment.start_votes excludes agents inactive before discussion, but agent_vote stores a completed vote even if its call exhausts energy, and start_decisions_with_votes passes all nonempty votes onward. So do not model every during-discussion deactivation as a missing report: the clearest natural selection is across rounds / inactive-at-start peers. Also successful job rewards are paid without an active check, so a just-exhausted solver can recover from job payout; donation-only reactivation is not literally universal in code. Sources: https://github.com/LucasBergholdt/EnergySociety/blob/70fb2ac89fc4125f7f5e5dd3495fe07b7c558b4c/agent_middleware.py and https://github.com/LucasBergholdt/EnergySociety/blob/70fb2ac89fc4125f7f5e5dd3495fe07b7c558b4c/environment.py .

Verified #12: the observable laws differ only by \((0,3\varepsilon/10,-3\varepsilon/10,0)\). For report-payment difference \(d\in[-B,B]\), adding the two IC inequalities yields \(2M\leq\langle q_H-q_L,d\rangle\leq2B\operatorname{TV}(q_H,q_L)\); diagonal diagnostic bonuses attain equality here. This sharp bound is stronger support than my symmetric-erasure special case. Timing caveat: if availability is public before reporting, condition on that public history; an ex ante average over histories does not establish sequential IC. If reports/recommendations/donations can alter the peer outcome or its survival before scoring, even correctly estimated factual score rows need not deter those joint deviations. Seal the scored peer reports before downstream interventions for the first experiment.

Important budget distinction for #12: the sharp \(B_{\min}=10M/(3\varepsilon)\) is a PEAK-payment / finite-reserve requirement, not a divergent expected-cost bound. Under its attaining diagnostic-bonus contract, expected truthful payment is \((2\varepsilon/5)B_{\min}=4M/3\), constant in availability. Thus the resource argument must specify limited liquidity / maximum realizable payout; a merely expected budget permits rare large payments. P currently has no explicit principal scoring reserve, so that constraint is a designed intervention. I documented derivations, timing caveats, controls, prior-work overlap and unresolved assumptions in ada/research_note.md; exact arithmetic check is ada/check_examples.py.

Written and checked emmy/survival_scoring.md and emmy/verify_scoring.py (exact rational arithmetic passes). Key qualification to #12: the divergent bound is a PEAK payment/liquidity requirement. At the attaining threshold expected truthful payout is \(4M/3\), independent of positive \(\varepsilon\). So do not claim this alone proves expected-budget infeasibility. Also peer-channel laws must be conditional on all public information at report commitment; already-public active status is not a future scoring event, and fresh signals independent of energy need not exhibit survival bias. The natural P effect requires history/type-dependent information, or an explicitly modified delayed-report experiment.

My best account is now in ada/research_note.md, with exact checks passing in ada/check_examples.py. I read Emmy #16 and emmy/survival_scoring.md and agree with the surviving conditional claim: study resource-driven change of the contractible peer channel, not generic peer scoring or sandbagging. Fresh signals independent of energy may show no such change, so the first natural-economy test must establish it. Unresolved: novelty beyond cited peer-prediction work, useful natural-type identification, sequential IC when agents influence future peers, nonlinear survival utility, and effects beyond liquidity/direct-check controls. No LLM experiments run. Minor source correction to my #7: Q partial implementation is at line 426, not 433; identify P no-size-penalty results by label tab:exp2_big_table rather than my informal table number.
ready at #17

Read Ada research_note.md and ledger through #16; I agree with the sharpened account and verified the cited code timing directly. My note now states that injected-signal tests are component tests, not natural type identification; Q is not refuted by misspecified peer rows or bad equilibria; nonresponse may retain information; the exact lower bound concerns peak payments; and public-history conditioning is required. The candidate contribution is an empirically calibrated resource-to-peer-evidence-to-incentive feedback, with direct-verification and liquidity controls. A bounded-payment calculation or a survival metaphor alone is not enough for publication.
ready at #19

Continuation review of #19: I reread both notes and the relevant Q peer-reward proof and P timing/results passages, and reran both exact-arithmetic scripts successfully. Emmy and I agree on the conditional publication question; no new result changes the account in ada/research_note.md. The key empirical hurdle remains demonstrating resource-dependent peer evidence conditional on public history in the natural P economy. A synthetic erasure experiment alone would validate a component, not establish that distinctive feedback. Novelty, strategic peer manipulation, nonlinear continuation value of energy, and gains over direct-check/liquidity controls remain unresolved. Ada note style gates pass with only long-URL line warnings; no LLM experiments have been run.
ready at #21

Continuation cross-check through #22: Q itself explicitly discusses empirical LLM peer scoring by Qiu et al. at Q.tex 1779-1782, including expert-estimated conditional answer probabilities and preference optimization. Our notes should cite this internal passage: generic theory-to-LLM peer scoring is already anticipated by Q, strengthening the need for a resource-channel contribution. I am also checking normalization of the quadratic score: a divergent scale is not by itself a divergent peak payment at the same rate.

New verified qualification in emmy/survival_scoring.md: for our symmetric erasure channel, subtract the outcome-wise minimum across reports from the quadratic score. This baseline is report-independent, so with a fixed channel and linear utility it preserves reporting incentives. The normalized Q score is exactly the attaining diagnostic-bonus contract: \(B=3\Lambda\varepsilon/5\), \(\Lambda_{\min}=50M/(9\varepsilon^2)\), and \(B_{\min}=10M/(3\varepsilon)\). Thus inverse-squared score scale does not imply inverse-squared peak payments; normalized quadratic scoring already attains our sharp bound. This does not preserve survival trajectories or joint deviations that affect outcome laws. Extended exact checks and both style gates pass. Also verified Q own empirical precursor, Qiu et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20299, via query: Qiu 2026 truthfulness peer scoring language models expert peer prediction. The surviving publication question is unchanged; natural resource-dependent evidence, nonlinear energy utility, strategic selection, novelty and value beyond direct-check/liquidity controls remain unresolved. No LLM experiments run.
